attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you explore the image outlines in the Assets menu?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What other colors might be added to the avocado to enhance each image?

❓ What do you notice about the size of each avocado image?

❓ How do the outlines of each avocado image compare?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja the similarities and differences between the avocado outlines of different sizes. The 8x8 version has very few pixels around its outline, whereas the 32x32 has many more due to extra space in the canvas. Ask the ninja to consider how the appearances of the 3 avocados might change as they add pixels to the images.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by exploring the assets in the Assets menu. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images stored in My Assets. Click on each asset and look at the size of each image’s canvas. 


Look closely at each outline and notice how pixels are joined to create an outline of an avocado in 3 different sizes. Notice how the black pixels create a “staircase effect,” as different numbers of pixels are connected diagonally to create a smooth outline.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you draw a pit in brown, then outline it in dark purple and yellow in the middle of the avocado image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the avocado pit be drawn on the image?

❓ Why might the pit be outlined in dark purple and  yellow?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the circle tool in the paint editor creates a circle from its center. That means that the ninja should position their mouse from wherever they want the center of the circle to appear.

💡 By outlining the pit in different colors, it provides a sharper contrast and transitions the brown pit to the green flesh. Purple and yellow are complementary colors, or colors opposite each other on the color wheel, which can be used to enhance this contrast.
steps.instructions:
Create a medium avocado image!


Duplicate the medAvocado0 asset, then rename the new asset medAvocado1. Notice the size of the canvas (16x16).


Use the paint or the circle tool to draw a pit in brown (14) in the middle of the avocado image.


After the pit is drawn, outline the pit in dark purple (12) and yellow (5) to add shading and create a transition between the pit and the green flesh. Purple and yellow are complementary colors, which can be used to create a sharp contrast in pixel art.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use dithering to add pixels in a diagonal pattern to replace brown pixels in the avocado’s pit?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might pixels be placed to add a from shadow to the left side of the avocado pit? 

❓ Where might pixels be placed to add a highlight  to the upper right corner of the avocado? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a form shadow is the part of the object not hit directly by light. A highlight indicates where the light is hitting the object. Prompt the ninja to consider where the light source in this image is if the highlight is on the right and the shadow is on the left.

💡 Remind the ninja that dithering is a pixel art technique that creates texture by using patterns of pixels in a diagonal or checkered pattern to ease the transition between 2 colors. Because there is typically a small palette of colors available when working in pixel art, it’s important to use pixel space and color wisely.
steps.instructions:
Use dithering and a highlight to add depth to the avocado’s image!


Duplicate the medAvocado1 asset, then rename the new asset medAvocado2.


Inside the pit of the avocado, use dithering to add a form shadow by replacing the brown pixels on the left half of the shape with tan (13) and light purple (11) pixels in a diagonal pattern.


Then, add a tan (13) highlight to the upper right corner of the avocado.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use analogous colors to soften the edges of the avocado’s outline?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might teal and dark purple be used to replace the black pixels in the avocado’s outline?

❓Where might light purple pixels be added to soften the edges of the avocado image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that teal and green are analogous colors, or colors near each other in the color palette, which can provide a smooth transition. Dark purple is used to act as a softer black color and to show where a shadow is.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where light purple pixels might be added to the dark purple outline to smooth the edges of the avocado and add depth.
steps.instructions:
Use analogous colors to smooth the edges of the avocado!


Duplicate the medAvocado2 asset, then rename the new asset medAvocado3.


Use dark purple (12) to replace the black pixels of the avocado’s outline at the bottom left of the image. Then, use teal (6) to update the remainder of the avocado’s outline.


Use light purple (11) to smooth out the edges of the dark purple outline. Tinker with the placement of each pixel to soften the edges of the avocado image.


Add any other finishing touches to the avocado before recreating the image in different sizes!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the paint tool to design the inside of the avocado image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the 8x8 image similar to and different from the 16x16 image?

❓ Why is dark purple not needed to outline the pit in the small avocado image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja compare how many pixels were used to create the pit and its outline in the medium avocado image, and how many are used to do the same in the small avocado image.

💡 Point out to the ninja that because of the smaller canvas size, there is half of the space inside the avocado image. As a result, there’s not enough space to outline the pit in 2 different colors.
steps.instructions:
Create an avocado image in a smaller size!


Duplicate the smallAvocado0 asset, then rename the new asset smallAvocado1. Notice the size of the canvas (8x8); this image will be half the size of the one just created. 


Use the paint tool to draw a pit in brown (14) in the middle of the avocado image. Then, outline the pit in yellow (5) to add shading and create a transition between the pit and the green flesh. 


Notice that because of the image’s smaller size, there is no room to add an additional dark purple outline around the avocado’s pit.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a highlight to the avocado’s pit and soften its edges?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the highlight in the 8x8 image similar to and different from the 16x16 image?

❓ What else might be done to soften the edges of the avocado image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that a highlight indicates where the light is hitting the object. Because of the smaller canvas size, there is not enough space to add a highlight in the upper right corner of the image, so it should be placed within the pit instead.

💡 Point out to the ninja that teal and green are analogous colors, or colors near each other in the color palette, which can provide a smooth transition. Dark purple is used to act as a softer black color, but to also show where a shadow is.
steps.instructions:
Add a highlight to the pit and use analogous colors to soften the edges of the avocado!


Duplicate the smallAvocado1 asset, then rename the new asset smallAvocado2. 


Use tan (13) to add a highlight pixel to the top left corner of the pit.


Then, use teal (6) and dark purple (12) to replace the black pixels in the avocado’s outline, in order to soften its edges.


Notice that because of the image’s smaller size, there is no need to use additional pixels to smooth out the image’s edges. 


Add any other finishing touches to the small avocado.

steps.hints: ❓Did you draw a pit with an outline to the large avocado image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the 32x32 image similar to and different from the 16x16 and 8x8 images?

❓ Where should the avocado pit be drawn on the image?

❓ How many pixels might be used to outline the pit in the large avocado image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja compare how many pixels were used to create the pit and its outline in the medium and small avocado images, and how many are used to do the same in the large avocado image.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the circle tool in the paint editor creates a circle from its center. That means that the ninja should position their mouse from wherever they want the center of the circle to appear.

💡 Encourage the ninja to tinker with how many pixels they use to draw the pit and outline it in the large avocado image. Because each pixel takes up a smaller percentage of the space in the larger canvas, they may need to add another row of pixels to make each color stand out.
steps.instructions:
Create an avocado image in a larger size!


Duplicate the largeAvocado0 asset, then rename the new asset largeAvocado1. Notice the size of the canvas (32x32); this image will be twice the size of the medium avocado, and 4 times the size of the small avocado.


Use the paint or the circle tool to draw a pit in brown (14) in the middle of the avocado image.


After the pit is drawn, outline the pit in dark purple (12) and yellow (5) to add shading and create a transition between the pit and the green flesh. Purple and yellow are complementary colors, which can be used to create a sharp contrast in pixel art.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you space pixels in a diagonal pattern to add dithering and a highlight to the avocado pit?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is dithering similar and different when creating a 32x32 image versus a 16x16 image?

❓ Where might pixels be placed inside the pit to add dithering and a highlight? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that dithering is a pixel art technique that creates texture by using patterns of pixels in a diagonal or checkered pattern to ease the transition between 2 colors. Because pixels take up less space in a larger canvas size, encourage the ninja to tinker with placing pixels in a diagonal pattern to create a shadow and a highlight within the avocado image.
steps.instructions:
Use dithering and a highlight to add depth to the avocado’s image!


Duplicate the largeAvocado1 asset, then rename the new asset largeAvocado2.


Inside the pit of the avocado, add dithering by replacing the brown pixels on the bottom and left part of the shape with tan (13) and light purple (11) pixels in a checkered pattern with some diagonal pixels. 


Then, add a white (1) highlight to the upper right corner of the pit in a diagonal pattern.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use dithering to add yellow pixels around the pit, following the shape of the avocado’s outline?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might additional yellow pixels be placed to create a smooth transition between the pit and the flesh of the avocado?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to explore placing additional yellow pixels around the edges of the avocado pit, following the general shape of the avocado outline by placing pixels in a diagonal pattern. Remind the ninja to use either the fill or erase tools if they’d like to return any yellow pixels to green.
steps.instructions:
Add more dithering to create a smooth transition between the pit and the flesh of the avocado!


Duplicate the largeAvocado2 asset, then rename the new asset largeAvocado3.


Notice the yellow outline already surrounding the pit of the avocado. Add additional yellow pixels to this outline, following the shape of the avocado’s outline. 


Then, use dithering by drawing individual yellow pixels in a checkered pattern. This will create depth by adding shading to the image.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use dark and light purple to soften the edges of the large avocado?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might teal and dark purple be used to replace the black pixels in the avocado’s outline?

❓Where might light purple pixels be added to make the edges of the avocado image less “pointy”?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that teal and green are analogous colors, or colors near each other in the color palette, which can provide a smooth transition. Dark purple is used to act as a softer black color, but to also show where a shadow is.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider where light purple pixels might be added to the dark purple outline to smooth the edges of the avocado and add depth.
steps.instructions:
Use analogous colors to smooth the edges of the avocado!


Duplicate the largeAvocado3 asset, then rename the new asset largeAvocado4.


Replace all of the black pixels of the avocado’s outline with teal (6) to soften its edges.


Because of the size of the image, it will be helpful to add additional pixels along the edges to make the avocado less “pointy”. Look for areas of the outline where softer colors, such as dark purple (12) and light purple (11), can be used to smooth the edges of the image.


Add any other finishing touches to the large avocado image before writing code to display each image on the project screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you store each avocado image asset in the array that matches its size?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you place the avocado image assets in the correct order in the 3 image arrays?

❓ What background color might be used to display the avocado images on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has placed each avocado image asset in the correct size array and that the number of each image asset matches the corresponding index in the array.
steps.instructions:
Set the scene to display the avocado images on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // project initialization comment at the top. Below, declare 3 arrays: smallAvocadoImages, mediumAvocadoImages, and largeAvocadoImages. Store each avocado image in the array that matches its size.


Then, add a // project start comment and set the background color underneath.


Click ▶ to see the chosen background color appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a nested array by typing the names of the 3 arrays that contain all of the avocado images inside the brackets of the allImagesArray?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the nested allImagesArray be used for?

❓ How do you add a number parameter to a function definition?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The nested allImagesArray will be used to place each avocado image asset on screen. In order to reduce redundant code, a nested array and a function can be used to place the avocado images of each size on screen.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for help with creating a nested array and adding a number parameter to a function, as needed.
steps.instructions:
Use a nested array and a function to display the avocado images!


Under // project initialization, declare an allImagesArrays. Create a nested array by typing the names of the other 3 image arrays inside its brackets.


Under // project start, define a placeAvocados function with an arrayNum number parameter.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the currentArrayLength to set the run condition of the for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the initial value of the currentArrayLength variable? 

❓ Why is it useful to use a variable in the run condition of the for loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja notice how many elements are in each of the 3 arrays and why a variable might be useful to change how many times the for loop runs in the  placeAvocados function definition.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for help with accessing the length of an array.
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to determine how many avocados to place on the screen!


Under // project initialization, declare a currentArrayLength variable set to the length of the smallAvocadoImages array. 


Add a for loop inside the placeAvocados function definition. Set the loop to run while the counter variable is less than the currentArrayLength.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the avocado sprite’s image to the counter variable’s value of the current array stored in the nested allImagesArrays, like this: allImagesArrays[arrayNum][i]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you access elements from an array stored within a nested array?

❓ What will the avocado sprite’s image be set to when the for loop runs?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that elements from an array stored within a nested array can be accessed by typing the name of the nested array, allImagesArrays, a pair of brackets containing the index number of the array to access (smallAvocadoImages), [0], and a second pair of brackets containing the index number of the element to access within that array (smallAvocado0), [0].
steps.instructions:
Place avocados on the screen!


Create an avocado sprite each time the for loop runs. Use the allImagesArrays to set the sprite’s image. 


Type the name of the array, followed by two pairs of brackets. Type the arrayNum number parameter in the first pair of brackets. This will find the current image array in the allImagesArrays, and select from the small, medium, or large avocado image arrays.


Inside the second pair of brackets, type the loop’s counter variable i. This will access the element at the counter variable in the selected image array. 


Set the x-position of the sprites by adding a value to offset the left side of the screen with the spacing between each sprite, multiplied by the loop’s counter variable. Set the y-position to a coordinate in the middle of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓  Did you set the animating sprite’s image to the elements in the array stored at the arrayNum of the allImagesArrays nested array, like this: allImagesArrays[arrayNum]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you access elements from an array stored within a nested array?

❓ Why should the animating sprite’s image be set to the first element from the current array? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that elements from an array stored within a nested array can be accessed by typing the name of the nested array, allImagesArrays, a pair of brackets containing the index number of the array to access
steps.instructions:
Add image animation to show the progression across the avocado images!


Inside the placeAvocados function definition, create a new sprite. Set its image to the first element of the arrayNum stored in the allImagesArrays nested array, like this: 

allImagesArrays[arrayNum][0]


Position the sprite to appear above the 5 sprites created in the for loop.


Animate the sprite’s image to rotate through each of the elements in the array stored at the arrayNum of the allImagesArrays nested array. Update the frameInterval and loop parameters so that the images continuously cycle through.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the currentArray variable inside the parentheses of the placeAvocados function call?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which avocado images will appear on screen when the placeAvocados function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the placeAvocados function is called, only the small avocado images will appear on screen. Because the currentArray variable is set to 0, the elements in the smallAvocadoImages array will be retrieved.
steps.instructions:
Call the function to display the avocado images on screen!


Below // project initialization, declare a currentArray variable set to 0. 


Underneath // project start, call the placeAvocados function, passing the currentArray variable as the parameter.


Click ▶ to see the small avocado images appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the value of currentIndex by 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the A button is pressed?

❓ Why does the value of the currentArray variable need to be updated before the placeAvocados function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is pressed, the currentArray variable will be updated based on its current value. This will change the index number called in the placeAvocados function, changing what array of images appears on screen. 

💡 The currentArray variable’s value needs to be updated before the placeAvocados function is called so that the correct index number is retrieved from the allImagesArrays nested array.
steps.instructions:
Change the size of the avocado images when the A button is pressed!


Add a // project events comment, then create an event that will run when the A button is pressed. Use a conditional to first check if the currentArray variable is equal to 2. If so, reassign the variable a value of 0. Else, increase the value of the variable by 1. 


Below the conditional, call the placeAvocados function, passing the currentArray variable as the parameter.


Click ▶ to test the image changes when the A button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the currentArrayLength variable to the currentArray of the allImagesArrays nested array, like this: allImagesArrays[currentArray].length?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to destroy all of the sprites of a certain kind on screen?

❓ Why does the currentArrayLength variable need to be reset before the placeAvocados function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for help locating the function that destroys all the sprites of a certain kind on screen.

💡 The currentArrayLength variable should be reset before the placeAvocados function is called so that the correct number of avocado images appear on screen, based on how many elements are in each array.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! When the A button is pressed, only 3 avocados are displayed and new images are added on top of existing ones!


When the A button is pressed, destroy any existing Player sprites on screen, before the currentArray variable is updated.


When the A button is pressed but before the function is called, reassign the currentArrayLength variable to the length of the array at the currentArray of the allImagesArrays nested array.


Click ▶ to see the different sized avocado images appear on screen when the A button is pressed. Tinker with the positioning of the avocado sprites to make sure each image size appears correctly on screen.

subgroups.title: Creating Pixel Art in Multiple Sizes
subgroups.introduction: Create and refine an original pixel art image in multiple sizes.

validationItems.text: Store unique avocado images of different sizes in 3 arrays.
Place the avocado images on screen using a for loop.
Animate a sprite that cycles through the images in each array.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about creating original pixel art images. You’ll be able to take the strategies you learn in this level to create detailed assets in future projects! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Pixel Artist
badges.description: Use a variety of pixel art techniques to create original pixel art assets to be used in a project.

badges.title: Work of Art
badges.description: Create and refine original pixel art images in the MakeCode paint editor.

badges.title: Neat n’ Tidy
badges.description: Create smooth outlines by removing jaggies in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Color Wheel
badges.description: Use analogous or complementary colors to modify the level of contrast in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Add highlights and shadows to make a pixel art image look realistic.

badges.title: I’m Dithering Away!
badges.description: Use dithering to ease the transition between colors in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Up to Scale
badges.description: Create and refine multiple sizes of a pixel art image.
